lesson.title: The Origin of Eukaryotes: Building Complex Cells Through Partnership
lesson.summary: Eukaryotic cells, with their nucleus and internal organelles, appear to have arisen when an archaeal host cell took on a bacterial partner that became the mitochondrion, a transition that remains an active area of research.
lesson.body:
Endosymbiotic theory explains where mitochondria and chloroplasts came from, but it leaves a bigger question only partly answered: where did the host cell itself come from, and how did it end up with a nucleus and the other features that define eukaryotic cells? This question, the origin of eukaryotes, is one of the most significant and still actively researched transitions in the history of life.

The leading current model proposes that the host cell was not a bacterium but an archaeon, meaning it belonged to the domain Archaea rather than Bacteria, even though both groups are structurally prokaryotic. At some point, this archaeal host took in, or merged with, an aerobic alpha-proteobacterium, the ancestor that (as covered in endosymbiotic theory) eventually became the mitochondrion. Because mitochondria allow a cell to generate energy far more efficiently than most prokaryotes can on their own, acquiring this partner may have been what made it possible for host cells to support the larger genomes and greater internal complexity that define eukaryotic cells. The exact sequence of events, and exactly why or how the merger happened, are still genuinely debated among researchers.

Some of the most compelling recent evidence about which archaea are closest relatives of the eukaryotic host cell comes from a group called Asgard archaea, identified and studied largely through genomic sequencing, with some members only cultured in the laboratory quite recently. Asgard archaea carry genes that are notably more similar to eukaryotic genes than those found in other archaea, making them a leading candidate for the lineage most closely related to the ancestral host cell. This is an active, fast moving area of research, and it is reasonable to expect the details to be refined as more evidence accumulates, rather than treating the current picture as final.

The origin of the nucleus itself is even less settled than the origin of mitochondria. One hypothesis suggests it formed through infolding of the host cell's own membrane, but this is one proposal among a few competing ideas, and it is fair to say this part of the story is less resolved than the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria, where the evidence is comparatively strong and consistent.

Chloroplasts entered the picture later, well after the basic eukaryotic cell, complete with nucleus and mitochondria, was already established. They arose from a separate, later endosymbiotic event: the engulfment of a cyanobacterium-like organism by the ancestor of plants and algae. Put together, the origin of eukaryotic cells illustrates something important about the eukaryotic cells you have already studied: many of their defining features were not built up gradually from a prokaryotic starting point through small incremental changes alone, but assembled in part through partnership between separate prokaryotic lineages, one becoming host and others becoming internal organelles.
